sections.title: Section A — Units I to IV (compulsory)
Section B1 — Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
Section B2 — Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Past adjustments — interest on capital and on drawings both omitted
questions.question: A and B share profits in the ratio 3 : 2, and their fixed capitals are ₹1,00,000 each. After the accounts were closed, it was found that both interest on capital at 10% p.a. and interest on drawings (A ₹2,000; B ₹1,000) had been omitted. The single adjusting entry is:
options: A) B's Current A/c Dr. ₹2,200; To A's Current A/c ₹2,200
B) A's Current A/c Dr. ₹17,000; To B's Current A/c ₹17,000
C) A's Current A/c Dr. ₹1,000; To B's Current A/c ₹1,000
D) A's Current A/c Dr. ₹2,200; To B's Current A/c ₹2,200
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) A's Current A/c Dr. ₹2,200; To B's Current A/c ₹2,200
Step 1: Interest on capital to be credited: A ₹10,000; B ₹10,000
Step 2: Interest on drawings to be debited: A ₹2,000; B ₹1,000
Step 3: Net appropriations omitted: A +₹8,000; B +₹9,000; total ₹17,000, which must be taken back from profit in 3 : 2 → A −₹10,200; B −₹6,800
Step 4: Net effect: A = 8,000 − 10,200 = −₹2,200; B = 9,000 − 6,800 = +₹2,200
Common mistake: Reversing the entry gives (A). Using the total of ₹17,000 gives (B). Looking only at the difference in interest on drawings gives ₹1,000 (C).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Share Forfeiture balance after re-issue
questions.question: After forfeited shares have been re-issued, the balance in the Share Forfeiture Account relating to those shares is transferred to:
options: D) Statement of Profit and Loss
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Capital Reserve
Why: The surplus on re-issued shares is a gain of a capital nature (money received on shares that was not refunded), so it is transferred to Capital Reserve, which is not available for dividend.
Why not the others:
(A) General Reserve is created out of revenue profits.
(B) Securities Premium is used only for premium received on issue.
(D) It is not a revenue income.
Key point: Forfeiture surplus on re-issued shares → Capital Reserve.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Paid-up capital — calls in arrears and calls in advance
questions.question: A company has 50,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, on which ₹8 per share has been called up. Calls in arrears are ₹6,000, and calls in advance received are ₹4,000. The paid-up capital shown under Share Capital is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹3,94,000
Step 1: Called-up capital = 50,000 × ₹8 = ₹4,00,000
Step 2: Less calls in arrears = ₹6,000 → paid-up capital = ₹3,94,000
Step 3: Calls in advance (₹4,000) is NOT share capital — it is shown under Other current liabilities until the call is made
Common mistake: Adding the calls in advance gives ₹3,98,000 (A). Ignoring the arrears gives ₹4,00,000 (C). Deducting the calls in advance as well gives ₹3,90,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Change in profit-sharing ratio — sacrificing ratio of two partners
questions.question: A, B and C share profits equally. They decide to share in the ratio 2 : 1 : 1 in future. The ratio in which B and C sacrifice their shares is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1 : 1
Step 1: A: 2/4 − 1/3 = 6/12 − 4/12 = 2/12 → gain
Step 2: B: 1/3 − 1/4 = 4/12 − 3/12 = 1/12 → sacrifice
Step 3: C: 1/3 − 1/4 = 1/12 → sacrifice
Step 4: Sacrificing ratio of B and C = 1/12 : 1/12 = 1 : 1 (together they give A his 2/12)
Common mistake: 2 : 1 (A) and 1 : 2 (B) assume unequal sacrifices. 3 : 1 (D) has no basis.
Key point: Equal old shares and equal new shares mean equal sacrifices.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Dissolution of partnership versus dissolution of firm
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Dissolution of a partnership does not necessarily mean dissolution of the firm.
(B) Dissolution of a firm necessarily involves dissolution of the partnership.
(C) A Realisation Account is prepared on the dissolution of a firm.
(D) Partners' Capital Accounts are closed before the Realisation Account is prepared.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why:
(A) True — on admission, retirement or death, the partnership is reconstituted but the firm continues.
(B) True — when the firm ends, every partner's relationship ends too.
(C) True — assets are realised and liabilities settled through the Realisation A/c.
(D) False — the capital accounts are closed LAST, after the realisation profit or loss has been transferred to them.
Why not the others: Options (A), (B) and (C) all include the false statement (D).
Key point: Firm dissolved ⇒ partnership dissolved, but not the other way round.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Goodwill — capitalisation method with accumulated loss
questions.question: A firm's partners' capitals total ₹4,00,000 and its reserves are ₹1,00,000. Its balance sheet also shows a debit balance of ₹20,000 in the Profit and Loss Account. The average profit is ₹60,000 and the normal rate of return is 10%. Goodwill by the capitalisation of average profit method is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹1,20,000
Step 1: Capital employed = Capitals ₹4,00,000 + Reserves ₹1,00,000 − P&L debit balance ₹20,000 = ₹4,80,000 (an accumulated loss reduces the owners' funds)
Step 2: Capitalised value of average profit = ₹60,000 × 100/10 = ₹6,00,000
Step 3: Goodwill = ₹6,00,000 − ₹4,80,000 = ₹1,20,000
Common mistake: Ignoring the debit balance gives ₹1,00,000 (A). Leaving out the reserves gives ₹2,00,000 (B). ₹6,00,000 (C) is the capitalised value.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Goodwill — weighted average with a loss and an abnormal gain
questions.question: A firm's results were: 2022-23 profit ₹40,000 (weight 1); 2023-24 loss ₹10,000 (weight 2); 2024-25 profit ₹1,00,000, which includes an abnormal gain of ₹20,000 (weight 3). Goodwill is valued at two years' purchase of the weighted average NORMAL profit. The value of goodwill is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹86,667
Step 1: Normal results: ₹40,000; (₹10,000) loss; ₹1,00,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹80,000
Step 2: Weighted products: 40,000 × 1 = 40,000; −10,000 × 2 = −20,000; 80,000 × 3 = 2,40,000; total ₹2,60,000
Step 3: Weighted average = ₹2,60,000 ÷ 6 = ₹43,333 (approx.)
Step 4: Goodwill = ₹43,333.33 × 2 = ₹86,667 (approx.)
Common mistake: Not removing the abnormal gain gives ₹1,06,667 (B). Treating the loss as a profit gives ₹1,00,000 (C). ₹43,333 (D) is the weighted average itself.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Presentation of debenture-related items
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II with reference to the balance sheet of a company as per Schedule III:

List-I (Item)
(A) 10% Debentures redeemable after 5 years
(B) Interest accrued but not due on debentures
(C) Premium on redemption of debentures, payable after 5 years
(D) Debentures Suspense Account (collateral debentures)

List-II (Presentation)
(I) Other current liabilities
(II) Deducted from the debentures to which it relates
(III) Long-term borrowings
(IV) Other long-term liabilities

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why:
(A) Debentures due after 12 months → Long-term borrowings (III).
(B) Interest accrued is payable soon → Other current liabilities (I).
(C) The redemption premium payable after 5 years → Other long-term liabilities (IV).
(D) Debentures Suspense is deducted from the collateral debentures, so the net is nil (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the debentures and the redemption premium; (C) swaps the accrued interest and the suspense account; (D) swaps the debentures and the accrued interest.
Key point: Principal → borrowings; extras payable later → other liabilities.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Goodwill — ratio used on different occasions
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Goodwill item)
(A) Premium brought in by a new partner
(B) Retiring partner's share of goodwill
(C) Existing goodwill written off
(D) Goodwill adjustment on a change in profit-sharing ratio

List-II (Ratio or basis used)
(I) Old profit-sharing ratio
(II) Sacrificing ratio
(III) Gaining ratio
(IV) Between the gaining and the sacrificing partners, in proportion to the gain or sacrifice

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(IV)
Why:
(A) The premium compensates those who sacrificed → sacrificing ratio (II).
(B) The partners who acquire the retiring partner's share pay for it → gaining ratio (III).
(C) Old goodwill belongs to the old partners → old ratio (I).
(D) On a change in ratio, each gaining partner pays each sacrificing partner for the share gained → (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the sacrificing and gaining ratios; (B) and (D) misplace the old ratio.
Key point: Who loses a share is credited; who gains a share is debited.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Revaluation Account — principles
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the Revaluation Account:
(A) It records the changes in the values of assets and liabilities at the time of reconstitution.
(B) Its balance is transferred to the old partners in their old ratio.
(C) Accumulated reserves are not passed through it.
(D) It is prepared only on the dissolution of a firm.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why:
(A) True — this is its purpose.
(B) True — the gain or loss belongs to the period before the change.
(C) True — reserves are transferred directly to the capital accounts, not through the Revaluation A/c.
(D) False — on dissolution a REALISATION Account is prepared; the Revaluation Account is used on reconstitution.
Why not the others: Options (A), (C) and (D) all include the false statement (D).
Key point: Reconstitution → Revaluation A/c; dissolution → Realisation A/c.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Accumulated profits on dissolution
questions.question: On the dissolution of a firm, the General Reserve appearing in the balance sheet is transferred to:
options: A) The debit side of the Realisation Account
B) The credit side of the Realisation Account
C) The partners' Capital Accounts in their profit-sharing ratio
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The partners' Capital Accounts in their profit-sharing ratio
Why: General Reserve consists of past profits belonging to the partners. It is not an outside liability, so it does not go to the Realisation Account; it is credited directly to the partners: General Reserve A/c Dr.; To Partners' Capital A/cs.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) Only assets and outside liabilities go to the Realisation A/c. (D) No cash moves.
Key point: Reserves → capitals; accumulated losses → capitals (debit).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Investment Fluctuation Reserve when market value rises
questions.question: At the time of a change in the profit-sharing ratio, the balance sheet shows an Investment Fluctuation Reserve of ₹10,000. The investments have a book value of ₹50,000 and a market value of ₹55,000, and they are to be shown at market value. The total amount credited to the partners' Capital Accounts (in the old ratio) as a result of these two items is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹15,000
Step 1: The market value is ABOVE book value, so no part of the reserve is needed to meet a fall → the whole ₹10,000 reserve is credited to the partners in the old ratio
Step 2: The increase of ₹5,000 is a revaluation gain → Investments A/c Dr.; To Revaluation A/c ₹5,000; it also reaches the partners in the old ratio
Step 3: Total credited = ₹10,000 + ₹5,000 = ₹15,000
Common mistake: Counting only the reserve gives ₹10,000 (A). Counting only the gain gives ₹5,000 (B). ₹50,000 (C) is the book value of the investments.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Commission to a manager and to a partner
questions.question: A firm's profit before any commission is ₹2,31,000. The manager (an employee) is entitled to a commission of 10% of the profit after charging his own commission. Partner X is entitled to a commission of 5% of the profit after charging BOTH the manager's commission and his own. The profit available for distribution among the partners is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹2,00,000
Step 1: Manager's commission (a charge, debited to the P&L A/c) = ₹2,31,000 × 10/110 = ₹21,000 → profit after it = ₹2,10,000
Step 2: X's commission (an appropriation) = ₹2,10,000 × 5/105 = ₹10,000
Step 3: Divisible profit = ₹2,10,000 − ₹10,000 = ₹2,00,000
Common mistake: Taking 10% and 5% without the 'after charging' adjustment gives ₹1,96,350 (A). Leaving out X's commission gives ₹2,10,000 (B). Taking X's 5% of ₹2,10,000 directly gives ₹1,99,500 (D).
Key point: A manager's commission is a charge; a partner's commission is an appropriation.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Profit and Loss Appropriation — share of profit
questions.question: The profit of A and B (sharing in the ratio 2 : 1) for the year is ₹90,000 before appropriations. The deed provides interest on capital of ₹12,000 to A and ₹8,000 to B, and a salary of ₹10,000 to B. A's share of the remaining profit is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹40,000
Step 1: Total appropriations before sharing = 12,000 + 8,000 + 10,000 = ₹30,000
Step 2: Divisible profit = ₹90,000 − ₹30,000 = ₹60,000
Step 3: A's share = ₹60,000 × 2/3 = ₹40,000
Common mistake: Forgetting B's salary gives ₹70,000 × 2/3 = ₹46,667 (A). Sharing equally gives ₹30,000 (C). Adding A's interest to his share gives ₹52,000 (D), but the question asks only for his share of the remaining profit.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Issue of debentures for consideration other than cash — at a discount
questions.question: A company purchased machinery for ₹2,70,000 and paid the vendor by issuing debentures of ₹100 each at a discount of 10%. The number of debentures issued is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 3,000
Step 1: Issue price = ₹100 − 10% = ₹90
Step 2: Number of debentures = ₹2,70,000 ÷ ₹90 = 3,000
Entry: Vendor A/c Dr. ₹2,70,000; Discount on Issue of Debentures A/c Dr. ₹30,000; To Debentures A/c ₹3,00,000
Common mistake: Dividing by the face value gives 2,700 (A). Multiplying by 0.9 gives 2,430 (C). 2,970 (D) has no basis in the data.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Hidden goodwill — other name
questions.question: Goodwill that is calculated from the capital brought in by a new partner, when the firm's goodwill is not given, is also known as:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Inferred goodwill
Why: Hidden goodwill is not stated directly. It is inferred (worked out) from the new partner's capital contribution, compared with the total capital of the firm.
Why not the others:
(A) Purchased goodwill is goodwill paid for when a business is bought.
(B) Negative goodwill (capital reserve) arises when the price paid is less than the net assets.
(D) Self-created goodwill is the general idea of internally generated goodwill.
Key point: Hidden = inferred = implied by the new partner's capital.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Admission — three old partners sacrifice equally
questions.question: Three partners A, B and C (sharing 3 : 2 : 1) take in D as a fourth partner with a one-fifth share. They agree that each of them will surrender an equal portion of profit to D. What will be the profit-sharing ratio of the four partners?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 13 : 8 : 3 : 6
Step 1: Each old partner gives 1/5 ÷ 3 = 1/15
Step 2: A = 3/6 − 1/15 = 15/30 − 2/30 = 13/30; B = 10/30 − 2/30 = 8/30; C = 5/30 − 2/30 = 3/30
Step 3: D = 1/5 = 6/30
Step 4: New ratio = 13 : 8 : 3 : 6
Common mistake: If D's share came from them in the old ratio 3 : 2 : 1, the answer would be 12 : 8 : 4 : 6 (B). (C) and (D) do not follow the agreed sacrifices.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Realisation of assets at a discount
questions.question: On dissolution, stock with a book value of ₹50,000 realised 20% less than book value, and debtors of ₹40,000 realised 90% of their book value. The total cash realised from these two assets is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹76,000
Step 1: Stock = ₹50,000 × 80% = ₹40,000
Step 2: Debtors = ₹40,000 × 90% = ₹36,000
Step 3: Total = ₹76,000 (credited to the Realisation A/c; the loss of ₹14,000 on these two assets is part of the realisation loss)
Common mistake: Taking debtors at full value gives ₹80,000 (B). Reducing both assets by 20% gives ₹72,000 (C). ₹90,000 (D) is the total book value.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Nature of partnership — partnership at will
questions.question: A 'partnership at will' is a partnership:
options: A) Formed for a fixed period of time
B) With no provision for its duration or for its determination, which any partner may dissolve by giving notice
C) Formed only for a particular venture
D) In which the partners have limited liability
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) With no provision for its duration or for its determination, which any partner may dissolve by giving notice
Why: Section 7 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 defines a partnership at will as one where no period is fixed and no mode of ending it is agreed. Under Section 43, any partner can dissolve it by giving written notice to all the others.
Why not the others:
(A) That is a partnership for a fixed term.
(C) That is a particular partnership.
(D) Ordinary partners have unlimited liability.
Key point: No fixed term + no agreed end → partnership at will.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Admission — premium for goodwill brought in kind
questions.question: A and B share profits in the ratio 3 : 1. C is admitted for a share that he takes from A and B in their old ratio. C brings ₹1,00,000 in cash as capital and a machine worth ₹40,000 as his premium for goodwill. The amount credited to A's Capital Account for goodwill is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹30,000
Why: The premium may be brought in the form of an asset. The asset is debited and the premium is credited to the sacrificing partners in their sacrificing ratio (here the old ratio, 3 : 1).
Entry: Machinery A/c Dr. ₹40,000; To Premium for Goodwill A/c ₹40,000 → Premium for Goodwill A/c Dr. ₹40,000; To A's Capital A/c ₹30,000; To B's Capital A/c ₹10,000
Step 1: A's share = ₹40,000 × 3/4 = ₹30,000
Common mistake: ₹40,000 (A) is the whole premium. Sharing it equally gives ₹20,000 (C). ₹10,000 (D) is B's share.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Presentation of share capital — order in the note
questions.question:
Arrange the following items in the order in which they appear in the 'Share Capital' note to the balance sheet as per Schedule III:
(A) Subscribed and fully paid
(B) Authorised capital
(C) Subscribed but not fully paid
(D) Issued capital
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (B), (D), (A), (C)
Why: The note moves from the widest figure to the actual capital: Authorised capital (B) → Issued capital (D) → Subscribed capital, shown first as 'Subscribed and fully paid' (A) and then as 'Subscribed but not fully paid' (C), the latter after deducting calls in arrears.
Why not the others: (A) puts subscribed before issued; (B) starts with issued; (D) reverses the two subscribed lines.
Key point: Authorised → issued → subscribed (fully paid, then not fully paid).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Forfeiture — premium payable in two instalments
questions.question: Shares of ₹10 each were issued at a premium of ₹3, payable ₹4 on application (including ₹1 premium), ₹5 on allotment (including ₹2 premium) and ₹4 on the first and final call. The holder of 100 shares paid only the application money, and his shares were forfeited after the call. On forfeiture, the amount credited to the Share Forfeiture Account and the amount debited to the Securities Premium Account are:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Forfeiture ₹300; Securities Premium ₹200
Step 1: Premium received with the application (₹1 per share) stays in Securities Premium
Step 2: Premium due on allotment (₹2 per share) was NOT received → Securities Premium A/c Dr. 100 × ₹2 = ₹200
Step 3: Share Capital A/c Dr. 100 × ₹10 = ₹1,000; To Share Allotment ₹500; To Share Call ₹400; To Share Forfeiture ₹300 (the ₹3 capital part of the application money)
Common mistake: Including the received premium in the forfeiture gives ₹400 (A). Reversing the whole ₹3 premium gives (B). (C) understates the capital received.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Final settlement — partner with a current account debit balance
questions.question: A and B share profits equally. On dissolution: B's capital is ₹40,000 and his Current Account shows a DEBIT balance of ₹5,000; General Reserve is ₹20,000; the profit on realisation is ₹12,000; and B took over furniture at ₹8,000. The cash finally paid to B is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹43,000
Step 1: Capital ₹40,000 − Current Account debit ₹5,000 = ₹35,000
Step 2: Add General Reserve share (½ of ₹20,000) = +₹10,000
Step 3: Add realisation profit share (½ of ₹12,000) = +₹6,000
Step 4: Less furniture taken over = −₹8,000
Step 5: Cash paid = 35,000 + 10,000 + 6,000 − 8,000 = ₹43,000
Common mistake: Ignoring the furniture gives ₹51,000 (A). Adding the current account debit gives ₹53,000 (C). Leaving out the realisation profit gives ₹37,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Re-issue as fully paid of shares forfeited while partly called
questions.question: A company forfeited 200 shares of ₹10 each when only ₹8 per share had been called and ₹5 per share received. The board later decided to re-issue these shares to a new buyer as fully paid-up shares for just ₹6 each. What amount will finally go to Capital Reserve?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹200
Step 1: Forfeited amount = 200 × ₹5 = ₹1,000
Step 2: The shares are re-issued as ₹10 paid up for ₹6 → discount = ₹4 per share = ₹800, debited to Share Forfeiture A/c
Step 3: Capital Reserve = ₹1,000 − ₹800 = ₹200
Common mistake: Ignoring the discount gives ₹1,000 (A). ₹800 (B) is the discount itself. Measuring the discount from the ₹8 originally called up (₹2 per share) gives ₹600 (C), but the new holder is credited with ₹10 per share.
Key point: The discount is measured against the paid-up value credited on re-issue.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Fluctuating capital — closing balance
questions.question: Partners' capitals are fluctuating. A's capital on 1 April 2025 was ₹1,00,000. During the year he introduced additional capital of ₹20,000 and withdrew ₹25,000. He was allowed interest on capital of ₹6,000 and a salary of ₹12,000, and his share of the firm's loss was ₹8,000. A's capital on 31 March 2026 is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹1,05,000
Step 1: Credits = Opening ₹1,00,000 + Additional capital ₹20,000 + Interest ₹6,000 + Salary ₹12,000 = ₹1,38,000
Step 2: Debits = Drawings ₹25,000 + Share of loss ₹8,000 = ₹33,000
Step 3: Closing capital = ₹1,38,000 − ₹33,000 = ₹1,05,000
Common mistake: Adding the loss instead of deducting it gives ₹1,21,000 (A). Ignoring the additional capital gives ₹85,000 (B). Ignoring the loss gives ₹1,13,000 (D).
Note: Interest and salary are allowed here, so the firm had profit before these appropriations and a loss only after them.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Application money — statutory minimum
questions.question: As per Section 39(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, the amount payable on application on every security must NOT be less than:
options: D) 5% of the nominal value (or such other percentage as SEBI may specify)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 5% of the nominal value (or such other percentage as SEBI may specify)
Why: Section 39(2) fixes the minimum application money at 5% of the nominal amount of the security, while allowing SEBI to prescribe a different percentage for listed issues.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are not the figure laid down in Section 39(2).
Key point: Application money ≥ 5% of nominal value (Companies Act); minimum subscription = 90% of the issue (SEBI).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Share capital — non-cumulative preference shares
questions.question: If the dividend on NON-cumulative preference shares is not paid in a particular year, the arrears of dividend:
options: A) Lapse and are not carried forward
B) Are carried forward to the next year
C) Are paid before preference capital on winding up
D) Are converted into equity shares
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Lapse and are not carried forward
Why: For non-cumulative preference shares, the right to dividend for a year is lost if it is not declared in that year. Only CUMULATIVE preference shares accumulate arrears, which must be paid before any equity dividend.
Why not the others: (B) and (C) describe cumulative shares. (D) has no basis.
Key point: Cumulative → arrears accumulate; non-cumulative → arrears lapse.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Interest on drawings — product method
questions.question: Using the product method, the sum of the products of a partner's drawings and the number of months for which each drawing remained outstanding is ₹3,60,000 (rupee-months). Interest on drawings is charged at 10% p.a. The interest on drawings is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹3,000
Why: Under the product method, each drawing is multiplied by the months it remained outstanding. The total (in rupee-months) equals one month's use of that many rupees.
Formula: Interest = Sum of products × Rate/100 × 1/12
Step 1: Interest = ₹3,60,000 × 10/100 × 1/12 = ₹3,000
Common mistake: Forgetting to divide by 12 gives ₹36,000 (A). Halving the result gives ₹1,500 (B). ₹6,000 (C) comes from dividing by 6 instead of 12.
Key point: Products are in months, so the annual rate must be converted to a monthly rate (÷ 12).

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Guarantee of profit — principles
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about a guarantee of minimum profit to a partner:
(A) The guarantee may be given by the firm or by one or more of the partners.
(B) The deficiency is borne by the guarantors in the agreed ratio (or in their profit-sharing ratio if no ratio is agreed).
(C) Unless stated otherwise, the guarantee relates only to the share of profit, not to interest or salary.
(D) The guaranteed amount must always be paid out of the firm's capital.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why:
(A) True — a guarantee may come from the firm (all the old partners) or from particular partners.
(B) True — the guarantors bear the shortfall as agreed.
(C) True — the guarantee is normally about the profit share alone.
(D) False — the deficiency is met by reducing the GUARANTORS' shares of profit; the firm's capital is not touched.
Why not the others: Options (B), (C) and (D) all include the false statement (D).
Key point: Deficiency = guaranteed amount − actual share, charged to the guarantors' profit shares.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Shares for consideration other than cash — securities premium
questions.question: A company acquired a building for ₹5,50,000 and paid for it by issuing equity shares of ₹100 each at a premium of 10%. The amount credited to the Securities Premium Account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹50,000
Step 1: Issue price = ₹110 → number of shares = ₹5,50,000 ÷ ₹110 = 5,000
Step 2: Share Capital = 5,000 × ₹100 = ₹5,00,000; Securities Premium = 5,000 × ₹10 = ₹50,000
Common mistake: Taking 10% of ₹5,50,000 gives ₹55,000 (B). ₹5,00,000 (C) is the share capital. ₹5,000 (D) is the number of shares.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Issue of debentures at par
questions.question: When debentures are issued for cash at par, which account is credited with their face value?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Debentures Account
Why: Debentures are a liability recorded at face value. Entry: Bank A/c Dr.; To Debentures A/c (through the Debenture Application and Allotment Accounts if money is received in instalments).
Why not the others:
(A) Share Capital is for shares only.
(B) Securities Premium is credited only if they are issued above par.
(C) Bank is DEBITED, not credited.
Key point: Debentures A/c always carries the face value.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Remuneration to partners — absence of deed
questions.question:
Assertion (A): In the absence of a partnership deed, a partner who devotes more time to the business than the others is still not entitled to any salary.
Reason (R): Section 13(a) of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 provides that, unless otherwise agreed, no partner is entitled to receive remuneration for taking part in the conduct of the business.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Why: Section 13(a) states the rule directly. Extra effort entitles a partner to remuneration ONLY if the partners agree to it, so without a deed, no salary is payable however much work he does.
Why not the others: (B) The Reason is the legal basis of the Assertion. (C) and (D) Both statements are true.
Key point: No deed → no salary, no commission, no interest on capital.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Transfer of assets at book value
questions.question:
Assertion (A): On dissolution, assets are transferred to the Realisation Account at their book values.
Reason (R): The Realisation Account is prepared to find the profit or loss arising on the realisation of assets and the settlement of liabilities.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Why: To measure the gain or loss on realisation, the account must compare what the assets were carried at (book value, on the debit side) with what they actually fetched (cash received, on the credit side). That purpose (the Reason) is why assets are transferred at book value (the Assertion).
Why not the others: (B) The Reason directly explains the Assertion. (C) and (D) Both statements are true.
Key point: Book value in, realised value in → the difference is the profit or loss on realisation.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Issue of shares for consideration other than cash — principles
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the issue of shares for consideration other than cash:
(A) No cash is received by the company for such shares.
(B) Such shares may be issued at a premium.
(C) When the assets are bought, the vendor's account is credited with the purchase consideration.
(D) Such shares may be issued at a discount.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: The consideration is an asset or a service, not cash (A). The purchase is first recorded as Assets A/c Dr.; To Vendor A/c (C), and the vendor is then paid in shares, which may be issued at par or at a premium (B).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — Section 53 prohibits issuing shares at a discount (except sweat equity), whatever the form of consideration. Options (B), (C) and (D) all include (D).
Key point: Non-cash consideration changes how the price is paid, not the rules on pricing.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Capital Reserve — use
questions.question: A Capital Reserve (for example, one arising on the re-issue of forfeited shares) is generally NOT available for:
options: B) Strengthening the company's financial position
C) Distribution to shareholders as dividend
D) Being shown under Reserves and Surplus
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Distribution to shareholders as dividend
Why: A capital reserve arises from capital profits, not from trading operations. It is kept to strengthen the company or to write off capital losses, and it is not distributed as dividend.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) are proper uses of a capital reserve. (D) is where it is shown in the balance sheet.
Key point: Capital profits → Capital Reserve → not available for dividend.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Death — deceased partner's share of goodwill
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

P, Q and R share profits in the ratio 5 : 3 : 2. R died on 31 July 2025. The firm closes its books on 31 March every year. On 1 April 2025, R's capital was ₹2,00,000, and the firm had a General Reserve of ₹60,000. R's drawings up to the date of death were ₹15,000, and interest on his drawings was ₹600. The deed provides that on the death of a partner: (i) interest on capital is allowed at 12% p.a.; (ii) his share of profit up to the date of death is based on the average profit of the last three years; and (iii) goodwill is valued at two years' purchase of the average profit of the last three years. The profits of the last three years were ₹1,50,000, ₹1,80,000 and ₹2,10,000. P and Q continue to share profits in their old ratio. R's executor is paid ₹50,000 immediately, and the balance is transferred to the Executor's Loan Account.

Question: What amount will be credited to R's Capital Account as his share of the firm's goodwill?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹72,000
Step 1: Average profit = (1,50,000 + 1,80,000 + 2,10,000) ÷ 3 = ₹1,80,000
Step 2: Firm's goodwill = ₹1,80,000 × 2 = ₹3,60,000
Step 3: R's share = ₹3,60,000 × 2/10 = ₹72,000
Common mistake: ₹3,60,000 (A) is the firm's goodwill. Using one year's purchase gives ₹36,000 (C). Using a 3/10 share gives ₹1,08,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Death — share of profit up to the date of death
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

P, Q and R share profits in the ratio 5 : 3 : 2. R died on 31 July 2025. The firm closes its books on 31 March every year. On 1 April 2025, R's capital was ₹2,00,000, and the firm had a General Reserve of ₹60,000. R's drawings up to the date of death were ₹15,000, and interest on his drawings was ₹600. The deed provides that on the death of a partner: (i) interest on capital is allowed at 12% p.a.; (ii) his share of profit up to the date of death is based on the average profit of the last three years; and (iii) goodwill is valued at two years' purchase of the average profit of the last three years. The profits of the last three years were ₹1,50,000, ₹1,80,000 and ₹2,10,000. P and Q continue to share profits in their old ratio. R's executor is paid ₹50,000 immediately, and the balance is transferred to the Executor's Loan Account.

Question: R's share of profit up to the date of his death is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹12,000
Step 1: Period = 1 April to 31 July 2025 = 4 months
Step 2: Profit for 4 months on the average basis = ₹1,80,000 × 4/12 = ₹60,000
Step 3: R's share = ₹60,000 × 2/10 = ₹12,000 (P&L Suspense A/c Dr.; To R's Capital A/c)
Common mistake: Taking a full year gives ₹36,000 (B). Using the latest year's profit of ₹2,10,000 gives ₹14,000 (C). Counting 3 months gives ₹9,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Death — interest on capital up to the date of death
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

P, Q and R share profits in the ratio 5 : 3 : 2. R died on 31 July 2025. The firm closes its books on 31 March every year. On 1 April 2025, R's capital was ₹2,00,000, and the firm had a General Reserve of ₹60,000. R's drawings up to the date of death were ₹15,000, and interest on his drawings was ₹600. The deed provides that on the death of a partner: (i) interest on capital is allowed at 12% p.a.; (ii) his share of profit up to the date of death is based on the average profit of the last three years; and (iii) goodwill is valued at two years' purchase of the average profit of the last three years. The profits of the last three years were ₹1,50,000, ₹1,80,000 and ₹2,10,000. P and Q continue to share profits in their old ratio. R's executor is paid ₹50,000 immediately, and the balance is transferred to the Executor's Loan Account.

Question: The interest on R's capital up to the date of death is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹8,000
Step 1: Interest = ₹2,00,000 × 12% × 4/12 = ₹8,000 (credited to R's Capital A/c)
Common mistake: Charging a full year gives ₹24,000 (A). Counting 3 months gives ₹6,000 (B). Counting 5 months gives ₹10,000 (C).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Death — amount transferred to the Executor's Loan Account
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

P, Q and R share profits in the ratio 5 : 3 : 2. R died on 31 July 2025. The firm closes its books on 31 March every year. On 1 April 2025, R's capital was ₹2,00,000, and the firm had a General Reserve of ₹60,000. R's drawings up to the date of death were ₹15,000, and interest on his drawings was ₹600. The deed provides that on the death of a partner: (i) interest on capital is allowed at 12% p.a.; (ii) his share of profit up to the date of death is based on the average profit of the last three years; and (iii) goodwill is valued at two years' purchase of the average profit of the last three years. The profits of the last three years were ₹1,50,000, ₹1,80,000 and ₹2,10,000. P and Q continue to share profits in their old ratio. R's executor is paid ₹50,000 immediately, and the balance is transferred to the Executor's Loan Account.

Question: After the immediate cash payment, what balance remains owing to R's executor and is carried to the Executor's Loan Account?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹2,38,400
Step 1: Credits: capital ₹2,00,000 + goodwill ₹72,000 + profit ₹12,000 + interest on capital ₹8,000 + General Reserve (2/10 of ₹60,000) ₹12,000 = ₹3,04,000
Step 2: Debits: drawings ₹15,000 + interest on drawings ₹600 = ₹15,600
Step 3: Amount due = ₹3,04,000 − ₹15,600 = ₹2,88,400; less cash paid ₹50,000 = ₹2,38,400
Common mistake: ₹2,88,400 (A) is before the cash payment. Ignoring the interest on drawings gives ₹2,39,000 (B). Leaving out the reserve gives ₹2,26,400 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Death — goodwill debited to the continuing partners
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

P, Q and R share profits in the ratio 5 : 3 : 2. R died on 31 July 2025. The firm closes its books on 31 March every year. On 1 April 2025, R's capital was ₹2,00,000, and the firm had a General Reserve of ₹60,000. R's drawings up to the date of death were ₹15,000, and interest on his drawings was ₹600. The deed provides that on the death of a partner: (i) interest on capital is allowed at 12% p.a.; (ii) his share of profit up to the date of death is based on the average profit of the last three years; and (iii) goodwill is valued at two years' purchase of the average profit of the last three years. The profits of the last three years were ₹1,50,000, ₹1,80,000 and ₹2,10,000. P and Q continue to share profits in their old ratio. R's executor is paid ₹50,000 immediately, and the balance is transferred to the Executor's Loan Account.

Question: How much of R's goodwill will Q have to bear through his Capital Account?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹27,000
Step 1: P and Q continue in their old ratio 5 : 3, so their gaining ratio is also 5 : 3
Step 2: Q's share = ₹72,000 × 3/8 = ₹27,000 (P's share = ₹45,000)
Entry: P's Capital A/c Dr. ₹45,000; Q's Capital A/c Dr. ₹27,000; To R's Capital A/c ₹72,000
Common mistake: Sharing equally gives ₹36,000 (A). Using Q's old share of 3/10 gives ₹21,600 (C). ₹45,000 (D) is P's amount.
Key point: When the continuing partners keep their old mutual ratio, gaining ratio = their old ratio.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Cash flow from investing activities — mixed items
questions.question: During the year a non-finance company: bought a patent for ₹50,000; sold land with a book value of ₹1,00,000 at a profit of ₹20,000; bought shares of another company for ₹60,000; and received interest of ₹5,000 on debentures it holds. The net cash flow from investing activities is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹15,000 inflow
Step 1: Outflows = Patent ₹50,000 + Shares ₹60,000 = ₹1,10,000
Step 2: Inflows = Sale of land ₹1,20,000 (book value + profit) + Interest received ₹5,000 = ₹1,25,000
Step 3: Net = ₹1,25,000 − ₹1,10,000 = ₹15,000 inflow
Common mistake: Taking the land at book value gives ₹5,000 outflow (B). Leaving out the interest gives ₹10,000 inflow (C). Ignoring the land sale gives ₹1,05,000 outflow (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Profitability ratios — gross profit ratio from mark-up
questions.question: A firm sells its goods at cost plus 33⅓%. Its gross profit ratio (on revenue from operations) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 25%
Step 1: If cost = ₹100, selling price = ₹133⅓ and gross profit = ₹33⅓
Step 2: GP ratio = 33⅓ ÷ 133⅓ × 100 = 25%
Common mistake: Taking the mark-up on cost as the ratio gives 33.33% (A). 20% (C) corresponds to a 25% mark-up. 66.67% (D) has no basis.
Key point: A mark-up of 1/3 on cost = 1/4 on sales; a mark-up of 1/4 on cost = 1/5 on sales.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Accounting ratios — form of expression
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Ratio)
(A) Inventory turnover ratio
(B) Net profit ratio
(C) Current ratio
(D) Average collection period

List-II (How it is usually expressed)
(I) As a pure ratio (e.g. 2 : 1)
(II) In times
(III) As a percentage
(IV) In days or months

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(IV)
Why:
(A) Turnover ratios measure how many times something is used → times (II).
(B) Profitability ratios are shown as a percentage of revenue → (III).
(C) Liquidity and solvency ratios are shown as a proportion, e.g. 2 : 1 → (I).
(D) The collection period converts turnover into time → days or months (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the turnover and profitability forms; (C) swaps the percentage and pure-ratio forms; (D) swaps times and days.
Key point: Times → activity; % → profitability; x : 1 → liquidity and solvency.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Profitability ratios — operating ratio and operating profit ratio
questions.question: A company's operating ratio is 82%. Its operating profit ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 18%
Formula: Operating ratio + Operating profit ratio = 100%
Step 1: Operating profit ratio = 100% − 82% = 18%
Common mistake: 82% (B) is the operating ratio itself. 12% (C) is an arithmetic slip. Adding instead of subtracting gives 118% (D).
Key point: Operating ratio measures cost efficiency; the operating profit ratio is what remains.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Operating profit before working capital changes
questions.question: A non-finance company's net profit before tax is ₹1,20,000, which includes dividend received of ₹8,000 and interest received of ₹4,000. Depreciation charged is ₹20,000, and there was a loss of ₹3,000 on the sale of furniture. The operating profit before working capital changes is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹1,31,000
Step 1: Deduct non-operating incomes (shown under investing): −₹8,000 − ₹4,000
Step 2: Add back non-cash and non-operating charges: depreciation +₹20,000; loss on sale +₹3,000
Step 3: 1,20,000 − 12,000 + 20,000 + 3,000 = ₹1,31,000
Common mistake: Adding the dividend and interest instead of deducting them gives ₹1,55,000 (A). Deducting the loss instead of adding it back gives ₹1,25,000 (B). Not removing the dividend and interest gives ₹1,43,000 (C).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Financial statements — purpose of the cash flow statement
questions.question: Which financial statement shows the inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents during a period, classified into operating, investing and financing activities?
options: C) Statement of Profit and Loss
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Cash flow statement
Why: Prepared under AS-3 (Revised), the cash flow statement explains the change in cash and cash equivalents between two balance sheet dates, activity by activity.
Why not the others:
(B) The balance sheet shows the position at a date.
(C) The Statement of P&L shows income and expenses on an accrual basis.
(D) A common-size balance sheet shows structure, not cash movements.
Key point: Profit is not cash — the cash flow statement bridges the two.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Financial statements of a company — Schedule III headings
questions.question: As per Schedule III, 'Capital work-in-progress' (a building under construction) is shown under:
options: C) Non-current assets — Property, Plant and Equipment and Intangible assets
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Non-current assets — Property, Plant and Equipment and Intangible assets
Why: Capital work-in-progress is a fixed asset still being built. Schedule III shows it as a separate line under the PPE and Intangible assets head of Non-current assets.
Why not the others:
(A) Inventories are goods for sale or production.
(B) It is not a current asset.
(D) It is not an advance; it is an asset under construction.
Key point: PPE, intangible assets, capital WIP and intangible assets under development all sit together.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Activity ratios — opening and closing inventory from turnover
questions.question: Revenue from operations ₹10,00,000; gross profit ratio 20%; inventory turnover 5 times. Stock at the end of the year exceeded stock at the beginning by ₹20,000. Find the value of stock at the END of the year.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹1,70,000
Step 1: Cost of revenue = 80% × ₹10,00,000 = ₹8,00,000
Step 2: Average inventory = ₹8,00,000 ÷ 5 = ₹1,60,000 → Opening + Closing = ₹3,20,000
Step 3: Closing = Opening + ₹20,000 → 2 × Opening + 20,000 = 3,20,000 → Opening = ₹1,50,000; Closing = ₹1,70,000
Common mistake: ₹1,50,000 (A) is the opening inventory. ₹1,60,000 (B) is the average. Using revenue instead of cost gives ₹2,00,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Cash flow statement — classification rules
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the cash flow statement:
(A) Depreciation is not a cash outflow.
(B) Purchase of goodwill is an investing activity.
(C) Proceeds from long-term borrowings are a financing activity.
(D) For a finance company, interest paid on deposits is a financing activity.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why:
(A) True — depreciation reduces profit without any cash payment, so it is added back.
(B) True — goodwill is a long-term asset.
(C) True — borrowing changes the firm's borrowed capital.
(D) False — paying interest on deposits is part of a finance company's main business, so it is an OPERATING activity.
Why not the others: Options (A), (B) and (D) all include the false statement (D).
Key point: The nature of the business decides how interest is classified.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Solvency ratios — from proprietary ratio to debt-equity
questions.question: A company's proprietary ratio is 0.75 : 1 and its total assets are ₹8,00,000. Its long-term debts are ₹1,50,000. Its debt-equity ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 0.25 : 1
Step 1: Shareholders' funds = 0.75 × ₹8,00,000 = ₹6,00,000
Step 2: Debt-equity = ₹1,50,000 ÷ ₹6,00,000 = 0.25 : 1
Common mistake: 0.75 : 1 (A) is the proprietary ratio itself. Inverting gives 4 : 1 (B). Dividing debt by total assets gives 0.19 : 1 (C).

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Generic considerations before sourcing accounting software
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the generic considerations before choosing accounting software?
options: B) Cost of installation and maintenance
D) The colour scheme of the software's screens
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The colour scheme of the software's screens
Why: NCERT lists the generic considerations as flexibility, cost of installation and maintenance, size of the organisation, ease of adaptation and training needs, the utilities and MIS reports available, the expected level of secrecy, the exporting and importing of data, and vendor support. Screen colours have no bearing on accounting needs.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are on the NCERT list.
Key point: Choose software for fit, cost, security and support — not appearance.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — text functions
questions.question: Which spreadsheet function joins the contents of two or more cells (for example, a first name and a surname) into one text string?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) =CONCATENATE()
Why: CONCATENATE(text1, text2, …) — or the & operator — joins text, for example =CONCATENATE(A2," ",B2) to produce a full name for a payroll register.
Why not the others:
(A) SUM adds numbers.
(C) MERGE is not a spreadsheet function (merging cells is a formatting command).
(D) LEN returns the number of characters.
Key point: Text functions — CONCATENATE, LEFT, RIGHT, LEN, UPPER.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — INT function
questions.question: A worker has completed 7.9 months of service, and only complete months count for a bonus. If B2 holds 7.9, what does =INT(B2) give?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 7
Why: INT rounds a number DOWN to the nearest integer, so INT(7.9) = 7. It is useful, for example, for finding complete months or complete units.
Why not the others:
(A) 8 is what ROUND would give.
(C) 7.9 is the original number.
(D) 0.9 is the fractional part.
Key point: INT → down to a whole number; ROUND → nearest.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Common errors in spreadsheet — IFERROR
questions.question: A ratio sheet uses =IFERROR(A1/B1,0). If cell B1 is 0, the formula returns:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 0
Why: IFERROR(value, value_if_error) returns the first argument unless it produces an error, in which case it returns the second. A1/B1 with B1 = 0 gives #DIV/0!, so IFERROR returns 0.
Why not the others:
(B) is the error that IFERROR suppresses.
(C) and (D) are not what the formula returns.
Key point: IFERROR keeps reports clean by replacing error codes with chosen values.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Payroll accounting — net pay after TDS
questions.question: Meena's salary slip shows: gross salary ₹60,000 (basic ₹30,000). Her employer deducts PF at 12% of basic, professional tax ₹200 and income tax at source of ₹4,500. What amount will be credited to her bank account?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹51,700
Step 1: PF = 12% × ₹30,000 = ₹3,600
Step 2: Total deductions = ₹3,600 + ₹200 + ₹4,500 = ₹8,300
Step 3: Net salary = ₹60,000 − ₹8,300 = ₹51,700
Common mistake: Forgetting TDS gives ₹56,200 (A). Calculating PF on the gross salary (₹7,200) gives ₹48,100 (B). Forgetting the professional tax gives ₹51,900 (C).

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Generic considerations before sourcing accounting software
questions.question:
Which of the following should a business consider before buying accounting software?
(A) Flexibility of the software
(B) Cost of installation and maintenance
(C) The expected level of secrecy (data security) required
(D) That the software is always the most recently released version
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: Flexibility (A), cost (B) and the expected level of secrecy (C) are among the generic considerations NCERT lists, along with organisation size, ease of adaptation and training, utilities and MIS reports, data import and export, and vendor support.
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — being the newest version is not a requirement; suitability, stability and vendor support matter more. Options (A), (C) and (D) all include (D).
Key point: The right software fits the business's needs and budget.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — HLOOKUP
questions.question: Cells A1, B1 and C1 contain the month names Jan, Feb and Mar, and cells A2, B2 and C2 contain their sales: 100, 150 and 120. The value returned by =HLOOKUP("Feb",A1:C2,2,FALSE) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 150
Why: HLOOKUP searches the FIRST ROW of the table for the lookup value (exact match with FALSE) and returns the value from the given row number in the same column.
Step 1: 'Feb' is found in column B of row 1
Step 2: Row 2 of that column holds 150
Common mistake: 'Feb' (A) is from row 1, not row 2. 100 (B) and 120 (D) are from the wrong columns.
Key point: VLOOKUP searches down the first column; HLOOKUP searches across the first row.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Payroll accounting — deductions
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Payroll deduction)
(A) Employee's Provident Fund contribution
(B) TDS on salary
(C) Professional tax
(D) Recovery of a salary advance

List-II (Nature)
(I) Income tax deducted at source for the Central Government
(II) Contribution to the employee's retirement fund
(III) Tax on employment levied by State Governments
(IV) Repayment of an amount paid to the employee earlier

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why:
(A) Employee PF → retirement savings (II).
(B) TDS → income tax deducted for the Central Government (I).
(C) Professional tax → a State levy on employment (III).
(D) Advance recovery → repayment of an earlier advance (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps PF and TDS; (B) misplaces TDS and professional tax; (C) swaps PF and advance recovery.
Key point: Net pay = Gross pay − (PF + TDS + professional tax + recoveries).

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Loan repayment schedule — monthly EMI
questions.question: A loan of ₹2,40,000 at 12% p.a. is to be repaid in 24 equal MONTHLY instalments. The instalment returned by =PMT(12%/12,24,-240000) is closest to:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹11,298
Given: Monthly rate = 12% ÷ 12 = 1%; number of payments = 24.
Formula: EMI = P × r ÷ [1 − (1 + r)^(−n)]
Step 1: (1.01)^(−24) ≈ 0.787566 → 1 − 0.787566 = 0.212434
Step 2: EMI = ₹2,40,000 × 0.01 ÷ 0.212434 ≈ ₹11,298
Common mistake: Ignoring interest gives ₹10,000 (A). Spreading simple interest of ₹57,600 evenly gives ₹12,400 (B). Using annual instalments (12%, 2 years) gives ₹1,42,008 (D).
Key point: For monthly payments, divide the rate by 12 and multiply the years by 12.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — ROUNDUP
questions.question: A rate in cell A1 is 12.231. A price list needs it rounded UP to one decimal place, so the formula =ROUNDUP(A1,1) is used. What does it display?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 12.3
Why: ROUNDUP always rounds AWAY from zero to the given number of digits, whatever the next digit is. To one decimal place, 12.231 becomes 12.3.
Why not the others:
(B) 12.2 is what ROUND or ROUNDDOWN would give.
(C) 12.24 is ROUNDUP to two decimal places.
(D) 13 is ROUNDUP to zero decimals.
Key point: ROUND → nearest; ROUNDUP → always up; ROUNDDOWN → always down.
